title: Degree: how connected is this vertex?

what.formal: The degree of a vertex is the number of edges incident to it; equivalently, the sum of its row in the adjacency matrix. In a hypergraph the degree of a vertex is the number of hyperedges that contain it — an edge of size five contributes one to each of its five vertices, not five to any one of them.
what.plain: A vertex's degree is simply how many relations it takes part in. On a plain graph, how many edges touch it; on a hypergraph, how many groups it belongs to.

what.md: **Why degree is the first quantity anyone computes.** It is the cheapest summary of a vertex's position. A vertex of degree 1 is an afterthought; a vertex of degree 3 is an organising hub. Almost every graph method begins by asking about degree, because degree controls how much information arrives at a vertex — and, as card 5 will show, how much a vertex needs to be damped down.

Two cautions. First, on a hypergraph a *size-five* edge adds 1 to each of five vertices: involvement is counted per relation, never per partner. Second, degree is a property of a vertex, so "this dataset has average degree 4.8" means "the average vertex belongs to 4.8 relations". Chapter 6's Table I prints exactly this quantity, and getting the direction of the count right there is the difference between reading the table and misreading it.

example.md: **Example 1 — read degrees straight off the picture.** Take the four-person graph from card 1: edges $\{1,2\}$, $\{2,3\}$, $\{2,4\}$.

items.md: Vertex 1 appears in exactly one edge, $\{1,2\}$. Its degree is **1**.
items.why: Count *relations*, not partners. Vertex 1 has one partner here, and one relation — they coincide only because the edges are pairwise.

items.md: Vertex 2 appears in all three edges. Its degree is **3**.
items.why: This is the hub. High degree means many messages will arrive here when information is passed along the graph.

items.md: Vertices 3 and 4 each appear once. Their degrees are **1** and **1**.
items.why: Total degree is $1 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 6$, which equals $2 \times 3$ edges. That is not a coincidence: every edge contributes exactly two endpoints, so the degrees always sum to twice the edge count. This handshake identity is the quickest sanity check on any degree list.

example.md: **Example 2 — the same count on a hypergraph.** Dorm 302 houses Zhang, Li and Wang, and that is the only relation recorded. Each student belongs to exactly one hyperedge, so each has degree 1 — even though the hyperedge has three members.

Compare the two examples. In the four-person graph, the total degree is 6 over 3 edges (two endpoints each). In the dorm, the total degree is 3 over 1 hyperedge (three endpoints). **The handshake identity changes shape on hypergraphs**: degrees sum to the sum of all hyperedge sizes, not to twice the edge count. Chapter 6's Table I has a column for each side of that identity.

quiz.q: A hypergraph has one hyperedge of size five. What is the degree of one of its five vertices?

opts.md: 5, because the edge contains five vertices
opts.expl: You have read the edge's size as the vertex's involvement. Size tells you how many vertices the edge holds; degree tells you how many edges hold this vertex.

opts.md: 1, because that vertex belongs to exactly one hyperedge
opts.expl: Correct. Degree counts the relations a vertex takes part in. This is precisely the distinction between the two degree columns of Table I: one counts vertices per relation, the other counts relations per vertex.

opts.md: It cannot be determined without knowing the other vertices' degrees
opts.expl: It can: degree is a per-vertex count and needs nothing but the edges that touch that vertex.

quiz.q: A graph has 5 edges and vertex degrees 2, 2, 3, 1 and $x$. What is $x$?
quiz.hint: Use the handshake identity: the degrees must sum to twice the number of edges.
quiz.sol: Twice the edge count is $2 \times 5 = 10$. The known degrees sum to $2+2+3+1 = 8$, so $x = 10 - 8 = 2$. Answering 5 is the common slip — that is the edge count, not the missing degree.

quiz.q: Why does a graph method usually treat degree-1 vertices differently from high-degree vertices?

opts.md: Because degree-1 vertices are always noise
opts.expl: Plenty of degree-1 vertices are meaningful — a paper cited by nobody else in the dataset is still a paper. Degree is about position, not about importance.

opts.md: Because a high-degree vertex would otherwise dominate the information its neighbours receive
opts.expl: Correct, and this is the motivation behind the degree normalisation the paper uses in Equation (1). If every vertex simply added up its neighbours' features, a hub with 900 neighbours would contribute 900 times as much as a leaf — not because it is 900 times more informative, but because it is 900 times better connected.

opts.md: Because degree-1 vertices cannot be represented in a matrix
opts.expl: They are represented perfectly well; their row simply has a single 1 in it.

close: **Where this is going:** degree is so central that the graph is often written down *as* its degrees and connections — which is what the incidence matrix of card 3 does, and what the paper's Equation (3) sums over.
